connector: In Chapter 16 you met General Hunter and the thousands of people who had escaped to Beaufort. Today you go back to one conversation: Harriet and the General, pages 152 to 155. Sort what anyone could check from what Sterling believes about it.

a.raw: the general laughed harder than harriet expected she grinned more widely at his answer
a.fixed: The General laughed harder than Harriet expected. She grinned more widely at his answer.
a.why: Capital T starts the sentence; capital G on General when it stands for one man’s title; capital H on Harriet; a period ends the first sentence; capital S starts the second. Harder and more widely compare.

b.raw: the children read more eagerly than ever the soldiers drilled more smartly each day
b.fixed: The children read more eagerly than ever. The soldiers drilled more smartly each day.
b.why: Capital T starts each sentence; a period ends the first. More eagerly and more smartly are comparative adverbs made with more.

fill1.h1: Medicine can lift a pain away. Which root means lift?
fill1.why: lev means lift: al + lev + iate = lift away, make lighter.

fill2.h1: A magician seems to make someone rise into the air. Which root means lift?
fill2.why: lev means lift: lev + itate = rise into the air.

fill3.h1: If you stand firm and won’t back down, which root means stand?
fill3.why: sist means stand: in + sist = stand firm on a point.

fill4.h1: A helper stands with you. Which root means stand?
fill4.why: sist means stand: as + sist = stand with, help.

g4w23cf1.h1: How did she walk compared with her brother? Quietly ends in -ly, so use more.
g4w23cf1.why: more quietly compares how two people walked.

g4w23cf2.h1: Soon is a short adverb. Add -er; don’t add more.
g4w23cf2.why: sooner already compares. More sooner doubles it.

g4w23cf3.h1: Hard is a short adverb. Add -er.
g4w23cf3.why: harder compares how hard he worked with everyone else.

g4w23cf4.h1: Of all of them means more than two. Use most, not more.
g4w23cf4.why: most carefully compares her with the whole group.

s4w23cf1.h1: Say abolish. Which vowel do you hear clearly after the b?
s4w23cf1.why: abolish has a loud o, so abolition keeps the o.

s4w23cf2.h1: Say cooperate. Which vowel do you hear after coop?
s4w23cf2.why: cooperate has an e, so cooperation keeps the e.

s4w23cf3.h1: Say define. Which vowel do you hear after the f?
s4w23cf3.why: define has an i, so definition keeps the i.

s4w23cf4.h1: Say separate. Which vowel do you hear after sep?
s4w23cf4.why: separate has an a, so separation keeps the a.

notes.wgrd: A biography mixes facts anyone could check with the author’s judgments about them. Mark the dates, places, names, and numbers. Then mark the words that rate a person or a choice.
vocab: To lift up; to raise to a higher level.
To stand against; to refuse to give in.
To keep going; to refuse to stop.
A person who worked to end (abolish) slavery.
notes.wordParts: lev means “lift” and sist means “stand”: elevate, lever, resist, persist.
notes.grammar: Never use more and -er together (more louder). And don’t use an adjective where you need an adverb: quicker should be more quickly.
notes.spelling: In a long word, one syllable gets the stress and is said loud and clear. A vowel in a quiet syllable often fades to a lazy “uh,” the schwa: ab·o·LI·tion. To spell it, find a related word where that syllable is stressed: a·BOL·ish.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: lifting, or standing?

why.t: At the end of Chapter 16, in the camp outside Beaufort, a woman pieces together an American flag from scraps of old clothing and says, “Our time is coming.” lev means lift, and sist means stand. Each right word sews one patch. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. lev = lift, sist = stand.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Back to Chapter 16 today, and back to one conversation. Harriet tells a Union general what Mr. Lincoln is getting wrong, and she does it with a story. Today’s question: which parts of this chapter are facts, and which parts tell you what Sterling believes?
transcripts.read: Read pages one fifty-two to one fifty-five slowly. Put the facts in one pile: names, places, numbers, the letter from Governor Andrew. Put the judgments in the other: words that rate a person or a choice. Then listen to the General’s letter to Congress. It’s funnier than you’d expect.
transcripts.spelling: Here’s the trick for lazy vowels. In abolition, you can barely hear the o. So find a relative of the word where that part gets the stress. Abolish. Now the o is loud and clear. Say the relative, and the spelling shows itself.

virtue.intro: In Chapter 16, people in Beaufort say, “We’s all free.” A soldier answers that they are not more than half free. Tap the moment that shows best what full freedom would take.
